segments.voice: Two cousins walk into the same bedroom, a few moments apart. Krishna is asleep in his palace at Dwaraka. Duryodhana arrives first and takes a fine seat at the head of the bed. Arjuna comes in after him and stands at the foot of the bed, hands folded. Both have come for the same thing: Krishna's help in the war that now looks likely. Both wait. Krishna wakes, and the first person his eyes fall on is Arjuna.
screen: `TWO COUSINS, ONE ERRAND.` → `THE HEAD OF THE BED, THE FOOT.` → `WHO IS SEEN FIRST?`

segments.voice: Udyoga is a Sanskrit word for effort, for getting ready, and this book of the epic is all preparation: for peace, if it can be found, and for war, if it can't. It started in Virata's hall, where the families talked it through. Balarama, Krishna's brother, said the Pandavas should ask gently, since Yudhishthira had chosen to play that game. Satyaki answered him hotly. King Drupada said: send an envoy, and gather allies too. So both sides go looking for friends, and both end up at Krishna's bed. Krishna makes them an offer. On one side, a huge army of his own fighting men. On the other, Krishna himself, alone, and he will not take up a weapon in the fight. Arjuna may choose first, he says: he saw him first, and he's the younger. Arjuna doesn't hesitate. He chooses Krishna, unarmed. Duryodhana is delighted. He gets the army, and leaves thinking he's won the better half. Now think about what each cousin was really asking for. Duryodhana wanted strength he could count. Arjuna wanted the person. This is one of the best-loved pictures of bhakti, devotion, in Hindu teaching. Many teachers put it simply: the devotee wants God himself, not only what God can give. Duryodhana walked away with the gifts. Arjuna walked away with the giver, and Krishna will drive his chariot when the war comes. And look back at the bedroom: one man sat at the head, where rank sits; the other stood at the feet, hands folded. It's why so many Hindus bow at the feet of the Lord.

segments.voice: Fold your hands, the way Arjuna stood at the foot of the bed. Softly say one name of God a few times, Krishna, or the name your family uses, breathing slowly, and this once, ask for nothing: no fix, no favor, just the one you're calling. If you don't pray, bring to mind someone you love, and notice that you want them, not what they can do for you.

segments.voice: An envoy rides into the Pandava camp. It's Sanjaya, the trusted charioteer and counselor of the blind king Dhritarashtra. He greets everyone warmly, asks after their health, and then delivers his master's message. It isn't an offer. It isn't a threat. It's a plea: don't fight. And something is missing from it. Dhritarashtra asks for peace, but he doesn't offer to give back what was taken.
screen: `SANJAYA RIDES IN.` → `THE MESSAGE: DON'T FIGHT.` → `WHAT THE MESSAGE LEAVES OUT.`

segments.voice: Sanjaya speaks movingly, and the Pandavas don't brush it aside. A war between cousins, he says, means killing your own teachers, your own uncles, your own kin. What kind of victory is that? Better, he says, to live on alms than to win a kingdom that way. Yudhishthira's answer is not angry. I want peace too, he says. Who would choose war if peace were possible? But peace has to mean something. Give us back our own kingdom, Indraprastha, the city we built. Then Krishna speaks, and gently turns the tables. Sanjaya's way sounds holy: give it up, walk away, beg rather than fight. But he's asking only one side to give anything up. And holding back, Krishna says, is no answer by itself. No one lives without acting. Even the gods act; the sun never rests from its work. A person must act, and act rightly. And then, in this same exchange, Yudhishthira makes a request so small it's almost painful to hear. Not the whole kingdom. Not even the city. Give us five villages, he says, and let this end. Five villages, from men who once ruled. Sanjaya carries the message home. Many readers hear in Krishna's reply an early sounding of the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna teaches karma yoga: don't run from your duty; do it rightly, and offer it to God. It's why so many Hindus treat ordinary work as worship. And Yudhishthira's five villages are karma yoga in action. Not a war cry, and not a shrug: the fairest, smallest act he can make.
screen: `SANJAYA: DON'T FIGHT YOUR KIN` · `KRISHNA: HOLDING BACK ISN'T HOLY` · `GIVE US FIVE VILLAGES` · then, large: `KARMA YOGA: ACT RIGHTLY`

segments.voice: Krishna decides to go to Hastinapura himself: one more try for peace, in person. Before he leaves, each of the brothers gives him a message, and several of them lean toward peace. Then Draupadi comes to him. She takes her long dark hair in her hand, the hair Duhshasana dragged her by in the dice hall, and holds it up. When you speak of peace, she says, remember this. If my husbands won't fight, my old father will, and my sons will. Krishna promises her she'll see justice, and sets off.
screen: `KRISHNA GOES HIMSELF.` → `DRAUPADI HOLDS UP HER HAIR.` → `REMEMBER THIS.`

segments.voice: Hastinapura gets ready for him. Duryodhana has rest houses built along the road and lays out a great feast. This is diplomacy as hospitality: if Krishna eats at his table, he's half won. Krishna passes the rest houses by. In the city he greets the old king, then goes to Kunti, the Pandavas' mother, who has been living in Vidura's house all these years. She weeps and asks after her sons, one by one. Only then does Krishna go to Duryodhana's palace. He accepts his greeting, and declines the meal. Duryodhana is offended. Why won't you eat with us? Krishna's answer is short and sharp. A person eats another's food either out of love, or out of need. You feel no love for me, and I'm in no need. So he walks back to a much plainer house: the home of Vidura, the wise half-brother of the king, who spoke up for the Pandavas years ago in the dice hall. That's where Krishna eats, and where he stays. This is the root of something every Hindu kitchen knows. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says: offer me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, with love, and I accept it. What God receives is the bhava, the feeling, not the size of the plate. That's why families offer food at the home shrine before anyone eats, and share it afterward as prasad. Duryodhana's banquet was a deal. Vidura's plain supper was love.
screen: `DRAUPADI'S HAIR GOES WITH HIM` · `A FEAST DECLINED` · `SUPPER AT VIDURA'S` · then, large: `A LEAF, A FLOWER, OFFERED WITH LOVE`

segments.voice: Morning in the great hall of the Kurus. Every seat is filled: Dhritarashtra on his throne, Bhishma, Drona, Vidura, Duryodhana and his brothers, Karna beside them. Krishna walks in, and the hall goes quiet. This is the moment the whole Udyoga has been building toward: a formal chance to stop the war, spoken face to face, in front of everyone who matters.
screen: `THE HALL IS FULL.` → `KRISHNA WALKS IN.` → `A CHANCE TO STOP THE WAR.`

segments.voice: Krishna speaks to Dhritarashtra first, and his argument is simple. You can stop this. Your sons and your nephews could stand together, and no one could stand against them. Peace would be your gain, not your loss. Give the Pandavas their share. Others speak after him. Bhishma and Drona urge Duryodhana to make peace. Duryodhana hears them, and refuses. He says, in effect, that he won't give the Pandavas even as much land as the point of a needle would cover, and he walks out of the hall. Then Gandhari, his mother, is sent for. He is called back to hear her, and she tells her son plainly that a person who can't rule his own anger and greed can't rule a kingdom. He leaves again. Outside, he and his friends make a plan: seize Krishna, tie him up, and the Pandavas will be helpless. Word reaches the hall. And Krishna laughs. The text says that as he laughed, his body blazed, and gods and heroes seemed to stream out of him, so bright the court had to shut their eyes. Only a few could look: Bhishma, Drona, Vidura and the sages, and Dhritarashtra, granted sight for that moment. Then the vision ends, and Krishna walks calmly out. Think about that. The one who could blaze like that came as a messenger, and asked. The night before, at Vidura's, he said he had come so no one could blame him for not trying. Many Hindu teachers point to this embassy when they say dharma tries peace first: a war fought by dharma comes only after peace has truly been offered. Krishna made the whole case in public, where no one could say it was never offered.
screen: `KRISHNA: PEACE IS YOUR GAIN` · `NOT EVEN A NEEDLE'S POINT OF LAND` · `A PLOT, A LAUGH, A BLAZING FORM` · then, large: `DHARMA TRIES PEACE FIRST`

segments.voice: Here is the secret. Karna is Kunti's son, born to her before she married Pandu. That makes him, Krishna says, the eldest brother of the five Pandavas. Then comes the offer. Come with me. Your brothers will touch your feet. You will be king, and Yudhishthira himself will stand behind your throne. Karna's answer is the heart of today. He says he already knows. Then he says why it changes nothing. His mother set him adrift as a newborn. A charioteer named Adhiratha found him, and Adhiratha's wife Radha raised him. Her milk fed him and her love kept him alive, he says, and he will not stop being her son for a crown. He married among the charioteer's people, and he has children there. And for years Duryodhana has stood by him when no one else would. He gave Duryodhana his word, and he means to keep it. Then he asks Krishna for one thing: don't tell Yudhishthira. If Yudhishthira learned that Karna was his elder brother, he would hand him the kingdom, and Karna would hand it straight to Duryodhana. Better that it stays secret. So a man is offered everything he ever wanted, and turns it down for the people who loved him first. In Hindu teaching, gratitude, remembering who held you up, is part of dharma, and so is keeping your word. Karna holds to both. But he holds them on Duryodhana's side, and that's the knot. Many teachers say Karna is right by one duty and ruinous by another, and the epic honors him and grieves him at once.

segments.voice: On the bank of the Ganga, a man stands facing east with his hands raised, reciting his prayers. The sun climbs until it burns his back, and he doesn't move. Behind him, a woman has come quietly and stands in the shade of his own upper cloth, waiting until he's finished. It's Kunti, and the man is Karna. Yesterday, Krishna asked Karna to change sides. Today, his mother comes to ask the same thing, in person.
screen: `PRAYERS ON THE GANGA BANK` → `KUNTI WAITS IN HIS SHADOW` → `A MOTHER'S REQUEST`

segments.voice: Karna finishes, turns, and greets her by naming himself: I am Karna, son of Radha and Adhiratha. What can I do for you? Kunti tells him the truth. You are not a charioteer's son. You are mine, and the Sun's. Come to your brothers. In the text, a voice even speaks from the sun to confirm her words. But his answer is hard to hear. You cast me away when I was born. You never gave me a mother's care. Now, on the eve of war, you come to me for the sake of your other sons. And then, after the hardest words, Karna gives her something. He won't join the Pandavas, but he makes a promise. In the battle he will not kill four of her sons, Yudhishthira, Bhima, Nakula and Sahadeva, even when he has them at his mercy. Only Arjuna will he fight to the end. Either way, he says, you will still have five sons: with Arjuna, or with me. Kunti embraces him, and they part. That's Karna. Earlier in the epic, Indra came to him disguised as a brahmin and asked for the armor he was born with, and Karna cut it from his own body and gave it. Many Hindus still remember him as Daanveer Karna, Karna the hero of giving. Dana, giving, is one of the oldest duties in Hindu life, and the Gita calls the purest gift the one given because giving is right, expecting nothing back. Karna can't give his mother what she came for. So he gives what he can, and it may cost him his life.
screen: `YOU ARE MINE, AND THE SUN'S` · `HARD WORDS, THEN A PROMISE` · `FIVE SONS, AND THE GIVEN ARMOR` · then, large: `DANA: GIVE WHAT YOU CAN`

segments.voice: The armies are drawn up on the field of Kurukshetra. In the palace at Hastinapura, the blind king Dhritarashtra sits and waits. Then the sage Vyasa comes to him with an offer. If you want to see the battle, he says, I'll give you sight. And the king says no. He doesn't want to see his own family killed. He only wants to hear about it. So Vyasa gives the gift to someone else: Sanjaya, the king's charioteer and counselor. Today the Bhishma book opens, and the Bhagavad Gita, which we've read before, comes back inside the story that holds it.
screen: `THE ARMIES ON KURUKSHETRA` → `THE BLIND KING REFUSES SIGHT` → `SANJAYA WILL SEE FOR HIM`

segments.voice: Earlier on the path we read the Gita verse by verse, as a teaching on its own. For these six sessions, we put it back where it lives: in the middle of a war report. After Vyasa's visit, the book doesn't go straight to the first morning of battle. Instead, Sanjaya comes back to the palace with terrible news. Bhishma, the grandsire of the whole family, has fallen. Days of fighting have already passed. Dhritarashtra breaks down, and then asks Sanjaya to tell him everything, from the start. So when the Gita opens with the old king asking what his sons and Pandu's sons did on the field of dharma, he is asking about something already over, the way someone asks after a funeral: tell me how it happened. Every word Krishna says to Arjuna reaches us through Sanjaya, spoken to a grieving father who refused to look. It's a report in a dark room, to a listener who chose to hear rather than see. And that's how most Hindus have met the Gita too: by hearing. The Bhagavata Purana lists nine ways of bhakti, and the first is shravana, hearing holy words and stories. It's why families play the Gita at home, gather for a katha, and listen at the temple even when the Sanskrit goes past them.
screen: `THE GITA PUT BACK IN THE STORY` · `THE TELLING STARTS AFTER BHISHMA FALLS` · `THE GITA, TOLD BY SANJAYA` · then, large: `SHRAVANA: HEARING IS DEVOTION`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and be a listener for a moment, not a watcher. Find the nearest sound, then the farthest one you can hear. Then, if you pray, listen to one holy word, Om or a name of God, said softly, or one verse of the Gita read aloud. If you don't pray, let the last sound be enough.
